newsitem.title: CHINA: IPO View-Strong sentiment seen aiding H-share IPOs.
newsitem.headline: IPO View-Strong sentiment seen aiding H-share IPOs.

text.p: Public offerings of Chinese enterprise H-shares are set to benefit from the recent enthusiasm towards the sector, sparked by hopes of an impending wave of corporate restructurings, analysts said.
"It (the strong sentiment) will aid the IPOs of H-shares," said Ricky Tam, senior analyst at Delta Asia Securities.

Though restructuring will not turn loss-making businesses into profitable ones in the near term, analysts said it would help the share price performances of listed companies and lift the response to new listings in the sector.

"It will for sure aid sentiment," said Eugene Law, director at Lippo Securities. "But still, I have reservations. We have to look back to the companies' business because many of them have disappointed the market in the past."
H-shares, Hong Kong-listed China-incorporated enterprises, had disappointed investors in the past by failing to gain even amid rallies in the overall market, the analysts said.

Institutions make up the bulk of H-share investors, with the sector attracting very little retail interest. Fundamentals have tended to drive the sector's performance and poor earnings outlooks for many of the companies had hurt sentiment. Analysts have said investors had overestimated the earnings recovery of H-shares and been burned.
"The sector had many chances to rebound in the past, but every time it moved up, the shares fell back," Tam said.
Now the sector is surging on expectations that reorganisations announced by two major constituents could herald a series of restructurings that will enhance profit-making potential.
The Hang Seng Chinese Enterprises Index rose 147.12 points or 14.71 percent to 1,147.01 last week, outperforming the blue chip Hang Seng index which gained 2.27 percent to 15,570.40.
Tsingtao Brewery Co Ltd last week said it had formed a new holding company aimed at rebuilding the beer maker's stock market image and boosting investor returns.
Shanghai Hai Xing Shipping Co Ltd said in recent weeks that its Shanghai-based parent would transfer control to a newly formed shipping giant held by the central government.
Analysts said Shanghai Hai Xing's restructuring in particular spurred hopes for asset injections by the new parent, and speculation that the model may be applied to other H-shares.
"The red-chip asset injection concept is seen coming to an end, and interest may be switching to H-shares," Tam said. "If Hai Xing proves to be successful, other H-shares will follow."
Red chips, Hong Kong-based companies with Chinese parents, have enjoyed great popularity due to speculation about asset injections, but appetite for that sector has cooled recently.
Brokers said investors particularly favoured the H-share outlook currently but warned that there was so far little change in underlying business realities.
"If investors continue to ignore the fundamentals, yes, it (the interest in H-shares) will continue," said Kent Rossiter, of institutional sales at Nikko Securities.
With the heat on, punters are eagerly looking forward to H-share initial public offerings (IPO), which, at other times, would not have whetted appetites.
Steel maker Angang New Steel Co Ltd is issuing 890 million H-shares in a public offer in Hong Kong. Its IPO closed on Friday and the shares are expected to begin trading on July 24.

Guangzhou-based airline group China Southern Airlines is seen kicking off its flotation in Hong Kong this week by issuing 1.03 billion shares at HK$3.75 to HK$4.75 per share, market sources said. Its IPO is expected to run from July 22 to 25.
Despite the strong sentiment in the sector currently, analysts said fundamentals would eventually prevail in investors' decisions.

"Restructuring induces a hope into the market that the sector is having a chance to rebound, but ultimately, people will look into the profitability and outlook of the businesses whether it is a listed firm or a new listing," Law said.
"Restructuring is not a magic touch," he added.
Overhauling the state-owned behemoths, many of which are involved in basic industries such as petrochemicals, steel and machinery, will not be easy, analysts added.

"This is very dangerous thinking since corporate restructuring is not an easy task as many of the H-shares are involved in single industries and are not as diversified as red chips," said Andrew To, dealing director at OSK Securities.
